16.canonical: Optimize for changeability and leave the codebase healthier than you found it: the real test of good code is how easily it can be changed, so favor clarity over brevity and write primarily for the future human reader.

18.canonical: Write for the reader, not the writer: code is read far more than written, so judge clarity from the viewpoint of another programmer who knows nothing about the system, and make code obvious with good names, consistency, and structure-revealing whitespace.

41.canonical: Simplify conditional logic: decompose complex conditions into intention-named functions, use guard clauses for unusual cases, and replace type-code switching with polymorphism — reserving polymorphism for type-based or base-plus-variant cases rather than converting every conditional.

50.canonical: Make testing risk-driven and bug-finding: concentrate tests on complex code and boundary/corner cases, start a bug fix by writing a failing test that exposes it, and judge a suite by confidence that a defect would trip a test rather than by coverage percentage.

53.canonical: Separate constructing a system from using it: move object construction and dependency wiring into main, factories, or a dependency-injection container so application objects stay passive and unaware of how they were built.

57.canonical: Eliminate duplicated knowledge so the system says everything once and only once: fold identical code into a method, repeated conditionals into polymorphism, and similar algorithms into a Template Method or Strategy.
